h: The New York Times page: 13 crore names, and one woman's face
dek: The world's most influential newspaper has made the striking of 13 crore names from India's voter list a full-page story; Deshkaal reads that page, from its photograph to its last line.
by: Mujib Mashal, Pragati K.B. and Hari Kumar
body: The photograph catches the eye first. On a Delhi street, four or five policewomen carry a young woman off, lifted into the air. Her body is sideways, one arm flung forward, her face clenched, teeth showing. Behind her are caps, uniforms, and somewhere a lathi (police baton). This is not a picture of violence but of defiance: someone refuses to leave her place, and the state lifts her and removes her. The paper tells the whole story through this picture, because that is the story too: people are being lifted out of their place, that is, out of the voter list.

The headline says 13 crore people in India have been wiped from the voter rolls, and there is anger over it. For its American readers the paper explains the number with a comparison: it is more than the entire population of Mexico. According to the report, from a list of about 97 crore names, more than two crore people were removed as dead and nine crore as 'absent, shifted and others'. Crores of names were flagged by an algorithm for 'logical discrepancies': things like the spelling of a name or the number of siblings. Many of those declared dead are now proving that they are alive.

The most serious part of the piece is its subheadline: the purge of errors and duplicates appears to target Modi's opponents. According to the paper, India's roughly 20 crore Muslims appear to be disproportionately targeted. In one constituency in Karnataka, about two thousand objections were filed in a single day last month, nearly half of them by just five people, and those whose names were objected to were overwhelmingly Muslim. Many forms were pre-typed, with only a blank left for the objector's name to be filled in by hand.

The most startling part comes from two senior officials who know the ruling party's strategy and spoke on condition of anonymity. According to the paper, one said the aim was simply to lock in an electoral advantage; the other said winning elections comes after a larger ideological goal. BJP spokesperson Pratyush Kant called it the noise of a weak opposition, and the Election Commission did not respond despite the paper's repeated requests.

The Bengal section sits in a corner of the page, but it weighs the most. There, about 90 lakh names were removed from the voter list, and right after that, in May, the BJP came to power for the first time in decades. The opposition has told the Supreme Court that in 82 of the 207 seats the BJP won, the number of deleted names was larger than the winning margin. Of the roughly one lakh appeals decided so far, most names were found to be valid. Court-appointed officers asked for 16 lakh names to be restored, but the Commission is appealing against their return.

The page rests on the voice of an ordinary man: Nanhe Lal, 43, who works in a toy shop in Delhi, reached a government office with his papers for the third time and said he would stand his whole family in front of the officials so they could see that we exist. And on the words of former Supreme Court judge Rohinton Nariman, that the heart of our democracy, the right to vote, is in grave danger.
nazar: What most of the country's TV channels have shied away from saying is now on a page of the world's most read newspaper, with a photograph, figures, the testimony of officials and the voice of a worker. There is shame in this and a lesson too: shame because we have to hear our own story this clearly from a foreign paper, and a lesson because journalism can still demand answers from power, if it is not afraid to ask questions.

The real story on this page is not the figure of 13 crore but Nanhe Lal. The vote is taken from those who have no papers, no leave and no lawyer: workers, migrants, Dalits, Adivasis (indigenous communities) and, most of all, Muslims. Like the woman in the photograph, they too are refusing to leave their place. The question is whether democracy will lift them and remove them, or make room for them.
sawal: When you have to prove that you exist, what is left of citizenship?
ref: SIR
The Special Intensive Revision of voter lists, in which every voter was asked for papers afresh. Critics say it put the whole burden of proof on the citizen.
Rohinton Nariman
Former Supreme Court judge and former Solicitor General of India, known for his clear views on constitutional rights.
ank: names removed from the voter list
seats in Bengal where deleted names exceeded the winning margin

h: Why is Modi shielding Gyanesh Kumar? The answer lies in UP
dek: Vir Sanghvi argues that worry over the Uttar Pradesh election is keeping the government behind an officer whose cost is being paid by the Prime Minister's own credibility.
body: Vir Sanghvi begins with Uttar Pradesh. In his view no state matters more to the BJP, and even the repeal of the farm laws in 2021 came from the fear of losing UP. Later the party's strategists considered that a mistake.

Then came 2024. The BJP's seats in UP fell from 62 to 33, its vote dropped from about fifty percent to 41, and it lost its own majority in the Lok Sabha. Now the UP election is a few months away, the party's internal surveys show a tight contest, and there is no big issue in hand. The writer asks whether Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar is the trump card the government is counting on.

There was an easy way out: send Kumar to some Raj Bhavan (governor's residence) or embassy and have him resign. Instead the government angered the young, turned Delhi into a fortress, faced accusations of ignoring the Supreme Court's directions on the metro and trains, detained lawyers, deployed more than thirty thousand personnel in central Delhi and went inside an aircraft to pick up protesters.

According to Sanghvi, the result is that opposition to Gyanesh is now turning into opposition to Modi. Any election Kumar oversees will have its legitimacy questioned, and even if the party wins, Yogi Adityanath will take the credit within it. He recalls that the Cockroach Janta Party has already forced Dharmendra Pradhan out, and that Rahul Gandhi is the biggest gainer from this tussle.

His advice is simple: the Prime Minister should say he has heard the people, and remove Kumar. The BJP can win UP even in a clean election. In the government and the party, hardly anyone apart from Kiren Rijiju and Ravi Shankar Prasad is speaking up for Kumar, and sending in paramilitary forces for every big protest cannot go on for long.
nazar: This voice matters because Sanghvi does not come from the camp sympathetic to the movement. When commentators who have been close to power also start saying that the price of saving one officer is the credibility of democracy, understand that the message has reached the court.

But one thing is missing from this calculation. The question is not only of winning or losing UP, but of the crores of people whose names were struck off the voter list. Whether or not Kumar keeps his chair, those names will have to be accounted for.
sawal: Is winning one state bigger than the credibility of an institution?
ref: Repeal of the farm laws, 2021
In November 2021 the government withdrew all three farm laws after a year-long farmers' movement. The UP election was then a few months away.
Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation
Education minister Dharmendra Pradhan had to leave office this year after the Cockroach Janta Party's Jantar Mantar protest over exam irregularities.

h: The face is Gyanesh's, but whose board is this?
dek: Rajendra Tiwari says that if the fight stops at one Chief Election Commissioner's resignation, the real machinery, from panna pramukh to delimitation, will stay just as it is.
body: The movement running since 2 October has brought the Election Commission's accountability to the centre of national debate. Rajendra Tiwari believes Gyanesh Kumar is an important character, but the problem neither began with him nor will end with his going. He lists a sequence, while taking care to say that a sequence is not in itself proof of a shared plan; it only calls for an inquiry.

The first link is the BJP's booth-level organisation. In Amit Shah's time a worker was placed on every page of the voter list, someone who knows the families, their castes and their leanings. It came out that missed-call campaigns had gathered data on about 25 crore people by 2019, and according to a 2024 report by Rest of World, the party's Saral app records religion, caste and even voter ID numbers.

The second link is the 2023 law. The Supreme Court had put the Chief Justice on the committee that selects commissioners; Parliament replaced him with a Union minister, giving the government two of three votes. Section 16 of the same law protects commissioners from lawsuits even after they leave office. Then came the SIR, in which, citing the Indian Express, more than 13 crore names were reported left out of the draft lists of 30 states and Union Territories. Two of the Commission's own commissioners recorded at least 14 written objections in ten months.
The writer's deepest worry is delimitation. The list decides who will vote; boundaries decide how much that vote weighs. Whoever has booth-wise data can redraw the map and predict results in advance.

So his demand is for records, not speeches: how strong is the wall between party and government data, who can change the list, and is there a pattern of one party benefiting from booth-wise additions and deletions of names.
nazar: This piece warns the movement of its biggest possible mistake: venting anger on one face and being satisfied. If the demand raised at Jantar Mantar does not reach the appointment law, an independent audit of the lists and the rules of delimitation, the next commissioner will sit in the same chair with the same structure.

The greatest danger is to those whose names are cut most easily: migrant workers, young people living in rented rooms, settlements on the margins. For them booth data is not a technical matter but proof of being a citizen.
sawal: Who will audit the voter list, and before whom?
ref: Panna pramukh
The BJP's booth system, in which one worker is responsible for each page (panna) of the voter list.
Election Commissioners appointment law, 2023
It removed the Chief Justice from the selection committee and put in a minister chosen by the Prime Minister. Its Section 16 gives commissioners immunity from legal action.

h: When the government itself staged a rail roko
dek: Oxford transport researcher Gaurav Mittal asks what keeping citizens away from the capital by halting the metro, buses and trains says about democracy.
body: In India, blocking the way is an old weapon of protest: farmers jamming highways, unions calling a chakka jam (wheel stop), and the rail roko (stop the trains) that goes back to the freedom struggle. Their force lies in halting daily movement so that power has to listen. Governments too have blocked movement, as with the trenches, concrete and nails on Delhi's borders in 2020-21.

According to Gaurav Mittal, 10 October was new in that roads, long-distance rail, local buses and the metro were all choked at once. The Home Secretary asked states to stop unauthorised entry, students from Pune were taken off a train, and young people were detained from the Goa Express at Itarsi. At first the plan was to shut 57 metro stations; after the Supreme Court stepped in, it came down to 45. In the writer's view, the fact that the court had to intervene shows how sweeping the steps were.

Those who were not part of the protest at all also paid a price: office-goers stranded in Gurgaon, sky-high taxi fares, patients and students. The writer calls this the reverse logic of rail roko. There, disruption is meant to make a demand visible; here, it is meant to stop the demand from gathering.

He sets three tests. First, proportion: the bigger and longer the restriction, the weaker its justification. Second, who bears the burden: those with flights and expensive taxis find a way, while for people who depend on public transport the journey simply ends. Third, access to what was blocked: Delhi holds Parliament, the Supreme Court and the Election Commission, and here geographical distance becomes political exclusion.

His conclusion is that transport is also the basic infrastructure of democracy. The right to protest can survive on paper while the road to using it is cut off. Governments manage huge crowds at religious fairs, elections and sporting events without shutting the whole network.
nazar: This is the side of the debate that is often missed. For someone who has no car and travels in the general coach, a cancelled train means the right to protest is taken away outright. Such restrictions cut off first the voice of the poor, the worker and the young person from a small town.
When reaching a capital is made difficult, the institutions sitting there also move just as far from the people.
sawal: Is the right to move not part of the right to protest?
ref: Rail roko
A form of protest in which people sit on the tracks to stop trains, used from the freedom movement to farmers' movements.
Mobility justice
The idea that the freedom to move, and its cost, do not fall equally on everyone, and that policy should take this inequality into account.

h: An undeclared emergency in the capital
dek: An editorial in Siasat, Hyderabad's Urdu daily, says all of Delhi was turned into a cantonment to protect one officer, and that this is a sign of the government's fear.
body: Siasat's editorial opens with a couplet and comes straight to the streets of Delhi. The paper says it was already expected that the Delhi Police and the central government would try to crush public protest to protect Gyanesh Kumar, and on Saturday that is what happened. The capital was turned into a police cantonment, and anyone who arrived was looked at with suspicion.

According to the editorial, leaders, Supreme Court and High Court lawyers, social activists, student leaders and journalists were all driven with the same stick. Protesters are alleged to have been beaten, dragged on the roads and packed into buses. The Jantar Mantar and Connaught Place area looked like a battlefield.

The paper makes special mention of the jostling of former chief ministers Mamata Banerjee, Pinarayi Vijayan and Arvind Kejriwal, along with Manish Sisodia, and also records the allegation that police entered the CPI(M) office. Trains coming to Delhi were stopped, 45 metro stations stayed shut despite the Supreme Court's objection, and CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were picked up from inside a plane that had come from Mumbai.

The editorial concludes that the government is scared and is throwing excessive force into saving one person, even though the protesters had repeatedly declared they would stay peaceful. The paper warns that young people will not be frightened into staying home like this.

In its last part the editorial turns to rising prices: rice, oil and vegetables have gone up, two meals a day are hard for many homes, and the government's attention is more on saving power than on relief. It calls for a concrete policy to control prices.
nazar: This voice from an Urdu paper deserves a hearing also because the communities that have lived through an undeclared emergency in their own neighbourhoods for years are the first to recognise it. The only difference is that the barricade has now reached former chief ministers and Supreme Court lawyers.
The turn to prices is not out of place either. For a home whose dal-rice budget has gone wrong, the vote is the last voice, and if that too is cut from the list, what is left?
sawal: Is it right to shut down a whole city for one officer?
ref: Siasat
An Urdu daily published from Hyderabad since 1949, counted among the oldest and largest Urdu papers in South India.
Undeclared emergency
In contrast to the declared Emergency of 1975-77, a situation in which civil liberties face the same kind of restrictions without any legal announcement.

h: Small signals, big storm: Shekhar Gupta's twelve warnings
dek: On Modi's 25 years in public life, Shekhar Gupta lists how small cracks can add up to a big crisis, and at the top of the list is the Election Commission's broken credibility.
body: As Modi completes 25 years in public life and supporters celebrate, Shekhar Gupta takes stock. In his view the third year of any term is the hardest, the cabinet is tired and incomplete, and Modi's three-part formula, Hindu-tinted nationalism, efficient welfare schemes and visible infrastructure, is under its greatest pressure since 2014.

He draws on management thinker C.K. Prahalad's idea of weak signals: small factors seem minor on their own, but together they weigh heavily. Number one on his list of twelve is the severe blow to the Election Commission's credibility. Number five is that two of the Commission's commissioners put their disagreement with the Chief Election Commissioner's decisions on paper.

The list also includes young people mocking the Prime Minister, and the CJP rising overnight to set the agenda from NEET to government schools, while the response of right-wing supporters stayed weak. Rahul Gandhi and the opposition getting space in mainstream media, questions over GDP figures, inflation, a weak rupee, unhappy allies, a stalled cabinet reshuffle and the difficult world of the Trump era are also on it.

According to Gupta, three foundations are under pressure: faith in the Constitution, the fairness of the higher courts and the independence of the Election Commission. He faults the Supreme Court for a wavering approach, as it weighs the Commission's credibility in the SIR case and the right to protest in the capital at the same time.

His words on the Commission are the harshest: it has never been this broken before, and this is a national crisis. The writer's estimate is that if Modi does not handle these questions, a major crisis could arise before the summer of 2029.
nazar: Shekhar Gupta is not seen as an open opponent of the government, so when he calls the state of the Election Commission a national crisis, the movement's core demand gets a mainstream stamp.

But in his list the young people on the streets are just one signal, like the stock market or the monsoon. In truth they are at the centre of this debate: it was they who carried the question of the Commission's credibility out of the drawing room to Jantar Mantar.
sawal: Is the Election Commission's credibility a bigger question than the other crises?
ref: Weak signals
An idea linked to management thinker C.K. Prahalad: that small, scattered signs together give warning of a big crisis.
National Interest
Shekhar Gupta's weekly column, published on ThePrint and also carried in Business Standard.
photo_note: Snowstorm: Hannibal's army crossing the Alps

h: Why is the government afraid of allowing protest?
dek: A Siasat editorial asks why, if the July movement stayed fully peaceful, every march is now being stopped on the way.
body: Published before the 10 October march, this editorial rests on one direct question: why is protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar not being allowed under any circumstances? According to the paper, wherever in the country a protest is attempted, the police foil it, and in Delhi even opposition MPs are being treated like ordinary citizens.

The editorial lays it out in order: on Gandhi Jayanti, lawyers, activists, student leaders and young people set out for Jantar Mantar, were stopped on the way and detained again and again. The same happened on the second and third days. Then when opposition parties came out, they were allowed to go neither to the Election Commission's office nor to Jantar Mantar.

The paper says such harshness is beyond understanding, and only one reason is visible: the allegations that the government got help from the Chief Election Commissioner in reaching power. In the editorial's view, the government does not want any action on vote theft or more facts to reach the public. This is the paper's own reading, and it stays within the bounds of an allegation.

The most powerful argument comes from a recent example. Two months ago the movement demanding Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation ran for more than a month, with no untoward incident, and ended peacefully as soon as its aim was met. According to the editorial, this makes clear that students do not want violence, and the government's present attitude only strengthens those very allegations.

The paper sees this as a double attack: on one side an alleged plan to take away the right to vote, on the other the suppression of the right to peaceful protest. It says citizens will let neither of these rights be taken.
nazar: This editorial was written before 10 October, and what happened that day proved its fears right. The July example is its strongest argument: a movement that peacefully won a minister's resignation is now being stopped as a threat.
The vote and protest, both rights are tied together. For someone whose name is cut from the list and who cannot even come onto the street with a complaint, what is left in a democracy?
sawal: What threat does the government see in a peaceful movement?
ref: Jantar Mantar
An area near Parliament that is Delhi's designated site for protests. In 2018 the Supreme Court lifted a complete ban on protests here.

h: Even if Hamas goes, where will the Palestinian question go?
dek: In the fourth year of the Gaza war, historian Lorenzo Kamel says a plan that ignores a century of dispossession cannot bring peace merely by removing Hamas.
body: The Gaza war is in its fourth year, and ceasefire talks are stuck on Israel's condition that Hamas first lay down its arms completely. Outside, the demand that Hamas leave Gaza is also gaining ground. Kamel says that even if this happens, it will not open a lasting path. He considers the 7 October 2023 attack a deadly mistake by Hamas, but calls Hamas not the disease but a symptom of long dispossession.

In the 1948 Nakba, hundreds of villages such as Najd and Huj were destroyed, and Israeli towns such as Sderot were later built on their land. The occupation began in 1967, when Hamas did not exist. It came out of the first intifada of 1987, and its founders Ahmed Yassin and Abdel Aziz al-Rantisi came from families driven out of villages that are in Israel today.

About half of Gaza's people are under 18, and more than half were not even born at the time of the 2006 election that Hamas won. In the Arab Barometer survey just before October 2023, only 29 percent of people in Gaza trusted the Hamas government and 73 percent wanted a peaceful solution. In the writer's view, calling the right to self-determination a reward for Hamas is therefore an old prejudice.

He also points to double standards. Palestinian groups are asked to meet conditions of recognition and giving up violence, Israel is not, even though Irgun and Lehi leaders Menachem Begin and Yitzhak Shamir became prime ministers despite violence against civilians. Hamas was nowhere in cases like the killing of Hind Rajab. The writer charges that Netanyahu finds Hamas useful because it lets him say there is no Palestinian worth talking to.
The conclusion is plain: with or without Hamas, the Palestinian demand for freedom will not end, nor will the question of security for people on both sides.
nazar: Even a year after the ceasefire, the debate on Gaza often stays stuck on what will become of Hamas. Kamel's piece reminds us that shrinking the question to one organisation is really a way of avoiding the history in which land, homes and the right of return were taken away.

India has for decades supported Palestinian self-determination and a two-state solution. At home too we know that when a long conflict is seen only through the lens of security, its roots disappear from view, and no peace lasts without touching the roots.
sawal: What peace can last without touching the roots of dispossession?
ref: Nakba
Arabic for 'catastrophe'. During Israel's creation in 1948, about seven lakh Palestinians had to leave their homes and hundreds of villages were destroyed. Palestinians mark it every year on 15 May.
Irgun and Lehi
Two armed Jewish groups active in British-ruled Palestine, which attacked the British and Arabs in the 1940s. Their leaders Menachem Begin and Yitzhak Shamir later became prime ministers of Israel.

h: Will clothes decide whose public space it is?
dek: Through three incidents, in a metro, a classroom and an airport, Shamsad Mortuza asks why a person's right to be present in Bangladesh should depend on moral policing of dress.
body: Shamsad Mortuza, vice-chancellor of the University of Liberal Arts Bangladesh in Dhaka, begins with three incidents. A sportsman on his way to the ground was stopped at a metro station for wearing shorts. At Dhaka University, a teacher was accused of asking a student wearing a niqab to change her seat out of fear that she might be a terrorist. The allegation has not yet been independently confirmed, but after protests the teacher was relieved of teaching duties and the English department nearly came to a halt.

The third incident stings the most. Three adult women travelling to Nepal with valid papers were stopped at the airport only because they were unmarried. Immigration officers questioned them about their clothes, their money and their marriage, and even phoned their families and the dean of one woman's university. The matter has now reached a High Court order.

According to Mortuza, public space belongs to everyone on paper, but its gatekeepers decide who gets to feel at home there. Women wear the hijab for many reasons, and women in Western clothes are harassed no less. The sportsman's case shows that men's bodies are policed too.

The piece also raises the question of class. One of the stopped women was reportedly asked how a farmer's daughter could go abroad. The writer asks why, if it is fine for a girl from a rich home to go to a beauty pageant, a farmer's daughter touring Nepal should grate. He speaks of an economy of feelings in which certain clothes automatically make someone dangerous.

He suggests that citizens examine their own feelings, that universities teach how to meet difference, that complainants be protected and the accused heard too. The rules of public spaces should be clear and open to all, so that a handful of people do not set the measure of respectability.
nazar: This debate is just as familiar on this side of the border. Whether it is hijab-wearing students stopped at college gates in Karnataka, couples policed in parks, or women travelling alone being questioned, each time someone gets the right to decide who is respectable.
Mortuza's most useful question is about class: the blow of policing falls hardest on those who are poor, women or minorities, and who have no shield of influence.
sawal: Who decides your right to be present in a public place?
ref: Moral policing
When police, officials or a crowd restrict people's clothes, relationships or movement according to their own morality, without any legal basis.
Affective economy
An idea from scholar Sara Ahmed: that feelings such as fear or hatred circulate in society and stick to certain faces, clothes or groups, turning them into signs of danger.

h: The Kartarpur corridor: a road to peace, shut from both sides
dek: Starting from the stalled journey of Pakistani Sikh pilgrims, Maham Sajid says both India and Pakistan treat pilgrimage not as a right but as a diplomatic switch.
body: On 11 September, about 100 Pakistani Sikh devotees stood at Faisalabad airport with valid Indian visas. They were to reach Hemkund Sahib via Sharjah and Delhi, since there is neither a direct flight nor a running train between the two countries. Immigration stopped them for lack of a no-objection certificate. Pakistan's Foreign Office said it had not even been informed of the visas and that the trip fell outside the 1974 agreement on religious sites.

Meanwhile, India had shut the Kartarpur corridor in May 2025, a few days after the Pahalgam attack, without giving any time limit. Indian devotees now have to get a Pakistani visa and go via Attari-Wagah. Oddly, in August the two countries extended the corridor agreement to 2029, yet the road stays closed.

Ramesh Singh Arora, Pakistan's first Sikh minister, says everything is ready on his side and India is responsible for the closure. He calls the Faisalabad case a paperwork gap, not a deliberate hurdle. But former parliamentary secretary Mahinderpal Singh has warned that he will reveal the names of the officers responsible. On 22 September, the anniversary of Guru Nanak's passing (Joti Jot Divas), Pakistani Sikhs took a nagar kirtan (religious procession) up to the zero line, while an Indian jatha (group of pilgrims) led by the acting jathedar of the Akal Takht was stopped before reaching the border.

The writer also offers a figure: of more than 6.8 lakh visitors to Kartarpur between late 2021 and 2023, Indians were less than a quarter, even though the corridor was built for them. Her argument is that both governments use pilgrimage like a diplomatic switch. A road that can be shut at any time by a one-sided decision is not a right, merely a concession.
nazar: When Kartarpur opened in 2019, it was called the most beautiful window of trust between the two countries. Today that window is hostage to politics on both sides, and the price is paid by elderly devotees for whom the Guru's door has become something to look at through binoculars.
The answer is a firm arrangement, binding on both sides, that keeps faith and travel apart from security tensions. Peace in South Asia is built from small bridges like this, not from big speeches.
sawal: Is pilgrimage a right, or a button in the hands of governments?
ref: Kartarpur corridor
A visa-free route opened in November 2019 that links Dera Baba Nanak in India to Gurdwara Darbar Sahib Kartarpur in Pakistan, where Guru Nanak spent his last years.
The 1974 protocol
An agreement between India and Pakistan on visits to religious sites, under which groups get visas for listed gurdwaras, temples and dargahs (shrines) on set occasions.

h: Deportation is now a weapon to silence critics
dek: On Latvia's move to expel Russian journalist Leonid Ragozin, Branko Marcetic writes that the Trump method is becoming the norm in liberal democracies.
body: Leonid Ragozin is an exiled Russian journalist who has lived in Latvia for more than a decade. Now Latvia has declared him unwanted and resolved to expel him soon. The foreign minister cited information from an unnamed agency, and the interior minister said plainly that Ragozin had expressed views against the country's interests. The trouble reportedly began with a podcast interview whose clips were spread by pro-war accounts.

According to Marcetic, calling Ragozin a Moscow mouthpiece is wrong. He has condemned the attack on Ukraine and Putin's rigged elections, and has written in defence of Navalny. His 'crime' is only that he questions Western policy, the effects of sanctions and simplistic readings of the war. Ragozin himself believes the government wants to avoid a case it cannot win in court.

The writer does not see this as a lone case. In the United States the Trump administration tried to deport pro-Palestinian activists such as Mahmoud Khalil and Mohsen Mahdawi for their views. In June France expelled the former head of RT France in the name of national security, without giving any public evidence. In Britain there were calls to strip Alaa Abd el-Fattah of his citizenship, and in Germany a climate activist faces a deportation case.

Marcetic's real concern is that the immigration system does not have the hearings and standards of evidence of a criminal court. That is why governments find this route easy: no charge to prove, no trial to fight. Once this was the mark of dictatorships; now liberal democracies are adopting it. And power changes hands: the weapon used today to expel one side's critics will tomorrow be turned on the other.
nazar: This story is no stranger to India. Visas of foreign journalists and scholars who criticise the government being cancelled, people turned back from the airport, threats to take away OCI (Overseas Citizen of India) cards: all this has been seen in recent years. These routes suit power precisely because no evidence has to be given in court.
Marcetic's warning is worth remembering: a weapon quietly accepted today against some disliked voice becomes tomorrow the rule for all dissent.
sawal: How is deportation without trial justified in a democracy?
ref: Persona non grata
A Latin phrase meaning 'unwelcome person'. By giving this status a country can stop a foreigner from coming or staying, often without giving a reason.
Mahmoud Khalil
A Columbia University student activist of Palestinian origin who was detained by US immigration authorities in 2025, which began deportation proceedings over his role in the campus movement on Gaza.

h: Trump's trade deals and the internet of the Global South
dek: EngageMedia's Prapasiri Suttisome argues that one condition in America's 'reciprocal trade agreements' could slow the spread of the internet in poorer countries.
body: One in three people in the world has no reliable internet, and this affects education, health care, jobs and even participation in democracy. This piece by a writer from EngageMedia appeared on Global Voices, and its concern is the US trade deals called 'Agreements on Reciprocal Trade'.

Since February 2025 the US has signed such deals with ten countries, including Malaysia, Cambodia, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Argentina and Guatemala. Most of them require partner countries to avoid suppliers that pose a security risk for infrastructure such as 5G, 6G, satellites and undersea cables. Some deals also say that which supplier is acceptable will be decided in consultation with the US. According to the writer, the targets are Chinese companies such as Huawei and ZTE, and the gain goes to American companies.

The trouble is that these countries still have a long way to go. Internet access is 53.4 percent in Bangladesh and 60.2 percent in Guatemala. More than one lakh schools in Indonesia have no internet. By the ITU's estimate, the world has to close a 1.6 trillion dollar gap in digital infrastructure by 2030, and a large part of this gap has so far been filled by cheap Chinese loans and equipment, even though questions of surveillance have also been raised about it.

Removing Chinese equipment is not easy either. The US itself managed to replace only 12 percent of Chinese equipment in its networks between 2019 and 2024, and the European Commission accepts that Chinese gear is 60 to 70 percent cheaper. The writer suggests that trade deals should encourage an open market with many suppliers, that countries be free to build their own domestic industry and acquire technology, and that each country choose its own equipment.
nazar: This piece shows that the bill for the technology race between great powers is often paid by the schools, hospitals and villages of poorer countries. The surveillance questions about China are real, but the answer cannot be to bind oneself to suppliers named by another country.
There is a lesson here for India too. In trade talks with the US, any condition on digital infrastructure will decide when, and at what cost, cheap internet reaches remote villages.
sawal: Whose security worries is cheap internet being sacrificed to?
ref: ITU
The International Telecommunication Union, the UN agency that sets telecom standards worldwide and gathers data on internet access.
Digital Silk Road
The digital part of China's Belt and Road Initiative, under which it gives loans and equipment to build fibre cables, mobile networks and data centres in other countries.

h: An economic policy blowing in the wind, weighed down by crony capital
dek: Economist Arun Kumar says government policy is busy only putting out fires, and its tilt towards favoured businessmen is leaving 94 percent of workers on the margins.
body: Arun Kumar says India's economic policy responds in a hurry to every new challenge but never even touches the basic disease. That disease is the tilt towards favoured capitalists. Without a level playing field, investors hesitate and many even head abroad. Elon Musk's recent charge that policymakers have bowed to oligarchic businessmen is, for the writer, a glimpse of this.

He lists how telecom, ports, airports and airlines are all shrinking into a few hands, while in space and defence, public bodies such as ISRO and HAL are being pushed aside. According to the writer, the biggest mistake is that policy is made with the organised sector and foreign markets in mind, while 94 percent of the country's workers are poor and unorganised. Caring only about a 6 percent market increases both inequality and dependence on outsiders.

His view on trade is also sharp. To escape American pressure, free trade agreements are being rushed through with Britain and the European Union, even though earlier agreements widened the trade deficit and weakened domestic production. He calls GST basically convoluted and shaped under pressure from big companies, with the evasion that is caught being only a tiny part of the real evasion.

He also questions the Reserve Bank's rise in the repo rate. In his view the root of inflation is disruption in the supply of food and fuel, not people buying more, so raising interest rates will only suppress demand further. Instead of collecting direct taxes from the rich and from companies, the government relies on indirect taxes, whose burden falls on ordinary people. His conclusion is that piecemeal reform will not work; the direction of policy has to change.
nazar: Amid rising prices of onions, sugar and rice, this piece reminds us that the heaviest burden of inflation falls on the unorganised worker, who is counted last when policy is made. High interest rates and indirect taxes both hit him hardest.

Crony capitalism is not just a moral question but an economic one. When the market shrinks into a few business houses, small traders, farmers and workers lose their bargaining power, and the ground of democracy weakens too.
sawal: When will the 94 percent of workers come to the centre of policy?
ref: Crony capitalism
An economy in which business success depends less on market competition and more on closeness to government, contracts, licences and concessions.
Repo rate
The interest rate at which the Reserve Bank lends to banks for short periods. When it rises, loans usually become costlier and demand in the market falls.

h: Six years in jail, honoured in Dublin: Umar Khalid wins the Front Line Defenders Award
dek: Former JNU student Umar Khalid, jailed for a peaceful movement against the citizenship law, has received the 2026 award for human rights defenders at risk; his father accepted it on his behalf.
body: The Irish organisation Front Line Defenders presented its 2026 awards at Trinity College, Dublin, on 8 October. The award for Asia and the Pacific went to Umar Khalid. Since he is in jail, his father Syed Qasim Rasool Ilyas attended the ceremony in his place.

The organisation said that while some see Umar as an enemy of the country, many see him as a voice of the people and a national hero. According to the organisation, he is being held in jail for leading a peaceful, democratic movement against amendments to the citizenship law that critics consider unconstitutional and anti-Muslim. Several international bodies, including the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention, have called his arrest unlawful.

This year's other four awardees are Laurinda Gouveia of Angola; Adda Victoria Caetano, a trans, Black Quilombola leader from Brazil; Ljubljana Nesic, a feminist peace activist from Serbia; and Ahmadreza Haeri, a Kurdish activist from Iran who has run a hunger strike campaign against the death penalty from inside prison. The award has been given since 2005, and winners also get help with security and advocacy.

The Delhi Police Special Cell arrested Umar on 14 September 2020. The police call him the main conspirator in the 'larger conspiracy' behind the 2020 northeast Delhi riots, and he faces several charges, including under UAPA, sedition and murder. Umar has always denied these charges. Just on 20 September, the Delhi High Court again rejected the bail pleas of Umar and Sharjeel Imam. In six years the trial has still not begun.
nazar: The world honours a prisoner as a defender of human rights, while in his own country his trial has not even begun in six years. That is the most painful part of this news: long imprisonment without a hearing has itself become the punishment, and laws like UAPA make bail almost impossible.

For the young people sitting at Jantar Mantar today for the right to vote, Umar's story is both a warning and a reminder: in this country the heaviest price for dissent is paid by those who are Muslim, and whose voices sting power the most.
sawal: If imprisonment without trial is not punishment, what is it?
ref: Front Line Defenders
An international organisation based in Dublin that works for the security of, and advocacy for, human rights activists at risk.
UAPA
The Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, under which bail conditions are so strict that accused people stay in jail for years without trial.

h: UN says Delhi detentions are worrying, free everyone now; India calls it interference
dek: The UN human rights office voiced concern over mass detentions before and during the Jantar Mantar protest; the Indian government called it unwarranted interference in internal affairs.
body: The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) said in a statement on Saturday, 10 October, that it was concerned by reports of the 'mass detention' of protesters, movement leaders, members of civil society groups, lawyers and journalists before and during the big protests in Delhi.

The office's spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan said the right to peaceful protest must be fully respected, and those arbitrarily detained must be released immediately and unconditionally. He also said any restrictions on protests must meet the tests of necessity and proportionality. According to the paper, this pointed to the barricades, internet shutdowns and cancelled trains in the capital.

The statement appealed to the police to exercise 'utmost restraint', and asked the government to hold meaningful dialogue on people's wider concerns. The Hindu writes that the UN office often issues reports, but such a direct appeal for dialogue with the government is unusual.

A few hours later, India's Permanent Mission in Geneva replied that India is the world's largest democracy, the Constitution protects the right to assemble, citizens exercise this right subject to reasonable restrictions for public order, and the courts are open for grievances. The mission called the UN's concerns 'unwarranted' and an 'unnecessary interference' in India's internal affairs.
nazar: The government's reply is the same old one: 'internal matter'. But when the world's biggest human rights body speaks about the detention of lawyers and journalists, it is not a statement of some foreign conspiracy but of the state of our own democracy. If everything is in line with the Constitution, why are the families of detained leaders not being told where they are?
sawal: A government afraid of its own citizens gets angry at whom?
ref: OHCHR
The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, in Geneva; its head at present is Volker Turk.

h: Old videos passed off as Jantar Mantar, exposed by a fact check
dek: Three videos spread as 'fresh images' of the 10 October protest turned out to be from July and September.
body: On 10 October the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and opposition groups had called a protest at Delhi's Jantar Mantar to demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The same day, three short videos began circulating on social media with the claim that they were from that day's protest. The fact-check website Boom examined all three and found the claim false.

The first video shows people carrying luggage, and the caption suggests the protesters had come prepared to camp for several days. A reverse image search showed it was from 28 September and showed students of Lovely Professional University going home after classes were halted following unrest on campus.

The second video was said to show chaos at Rajiv Chowk metro station, with the claim that crowds were stranded because the metro was shut on 10 October. According to Boom, the clip was posted on Instagram on 20 July. In the third video a man says police had placed broken-down vehicles before the protest. This too turned out to be from 21 July, when the CJP held a sit-in and a march to Parliament over the NEET paper leak.

Boom also noted that on 10 October Delhi was on high alert, 57 metro stations were shut and many trains had been stopped. In other words, the real situation was news in itself, yet old videos were used to build a new story.
nazar: On the day of a big movement, truth and rumour run side by side. Whether old videos spread in favour of a protest or against it, the damage is to the movement's credibility and to public understanding. When governments shut the internet and detain journalists, the work of fact-checkers becomes even more vital. The lesson for readers is simple: do not forward any video without asking its date and place.
sawal: Do you check a video's date before forwarding it?
ref: Reverse image search
A way of searching the internet for a picture or a video frame to find its earliest version. It shows when and where the material first appeared.
Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)
A new political platform of young people that called big protests in Delhi this year over the NEET paper leak and the Election Commission.

h: Accused in the Junaid-Nasir killings now threatens protesters
dek: Bajrang Dal-linked Monu Manesar issued a direct warning to CJP protesters in an Instagram video, while claiming to know nothing of police excesses.
body: According to a Newslaundry report, Bajrang Dal leader Monu Yadav alias Monu Manesar, who calls himself a gaurakshak (cow protector), posted a video of about two and a quarter minutes on Instagram on 9 October. In it he warned those coming to the CJP protest on 10 October that if anyone raised a hand against the police, his team would step in and deal with such people. His verified account has about one and a half lakh followers, and the video was viewed more than one lakh thirty-three thousand times in 24 hours.

Speaking on the phone from Gurugram, Manesar said his team would reach Jantar Mantar. When asked about police harshness towards protesters, he said he had heard of it but had not seen any video in which the police had touched anyone.

The report also recalls Manesar's past record. In February 2023 the bodies of Junaid and Nasir were found in a burnt vehicle at Loharu in Bhiwani. The families of both allege that six men of the Haryana Bajrang Dal, including Manesar, abducted them and burnt them alive. Manesar was absconding for more than five months. In September 2023 he was arrested in a case over provocative posts, and police said a pistol had been recovered. According to the report, he was released from jail on 8 March this year after about two years.

Newslaundry also notes that after Haryana's cow slaughter law was made stricter in 2019, about 600 FIRs were filed in Nuh alone between 2019 and 2022, and families in the area kept complaining of harassment by cow vigilantes. On the day this threat came, the Delhi Police were using loudspeakers to warn ordinary people not to disturb law and order.
nazar: This story is a picture of double standards. On one side, students, farmers and journalists who came out for a peaceful protest were being detained; on the other, a man facing serious murder charges was openly announcing that he would send in a private 'team'. Keeping law and order is the job of the police, not of any self-appointed squad. Muslim families in Nuh and Mewat have lived with this fear for years; now the same threat has reached democratic protest.
sawal: When will the police act on threats from private squads?
ref: Junaid-Nasir killings
In February 2023 the burnt bodies of two young Muslim men from Bharatpur in Rajasthan were found in Bhiwani, Haryana. The families accused cow vigilantes of abducting and killing them.
Nuh
A Muslim-majority district in Haryana, also called Mewat. There have been reports here of violence in the name of cow protection and of communal clashes in 2023.

h: Erode: a Dalit burial blocked, two men forced to fall at others' feet
dek: Even in a burial ground opened to all by the tehsildar's order, a Dalit family needed a police guard to bury their dead.
body: Another case of caste discrimination has come to light from Perumpalli village in the Perundurai area of Tamil Nadu's Erode district. According to The Mooknayak, Chenni, a 90-year-old Dalit elder of the village, died of an age-related illness on 5 October. When his family and community took the body to the village's public burial ground, some people from a backward class strongly objected, and it turned into a heated clash.

More than a hundred Scheduled Caste people live in the village. The report says that for a long time they had to take their dead about five kilometres away to Thingalur for burial. After a recent survey, the Perundurai tehsildar (revenue officer) had declared the burial ground open to all communities. Even so, the burial could be completed only under heavy arrangements by the revenue department and police.

It is alleged that during the clash Dalits were threatened not to come to the dominant community for any work in future. Right after that, two Dalit men were forced to fall at the feet of people from the dominant caste. A video of this spread fast on social media and sparked public anger.

On the night of 8 October, on a complaint by the revenue inspector, a case was registered at Thingalur police station against two people under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, and the investigation is on. P. Eswaran, the BSP's western region coordinator, condemned the incident. He called the threat to deny work an exploitation of Dalits' economic helplessness, and also questioned the role of the police and revenue officials present at the spot.
nazar: This incident shows that a right granted on paper does not land on the ground by itself. Officials were present, yet two men were made to bow in front of everyone. The most painful part is the threat to take away livelihoods, because farm labour in the village is still largely in the hands of dominant castes. If the accountability of the officials present is not fixed along with the FIR, the next burial will again happen in the same fear.
sawal: Why does equality need a police guard even after death?
ref: SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989
A law that treats humiliation, boycott and violence against Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe people as special offences. Stopping them from using public places is also an offence under it.

h: Nine dead in 24 hours in Manipur, now a Kuki-Naga clash
dek: Firing, ambushes and arson in Kamjong, Kangpokpi and Ukhrul; 14 houses burnt in Chassad.
body: On a day when the country's attention was on the Delhi protests, nine people were killed in three districts of Manipur between Friday and Saturday. Scroll reported this citing the Hindustan Times, based on statements by police officials. The police also confirmed the Kangpokpi deaths directly to Scroll.

The violence began on Friday night in Chassad, a Kuki-majority village in the Naga-majority Kamjong district. Security forces caught some 'village volunteers', after which there was firing, and a 42-year-old mother of five was killed by a bullet near her neck. Then firing broke out between Kuki and Naga armed groups, a 22-year-old man was killed and at least 14 houses of both communities were set on fire. Prohibitory orders were imposed within 400 metres of the police station. In the same district, two more people were killed in an attack on Ningchou, a Tangkhul Naga village near the Myanmar border.

On Saturday, in Kangpokpi, a Naga village guard was killed and two were injured in firing by suspected Kuki militants on the Imphal-Tamenglong road. In the morning three more village guards lost their lives at Makui. In Ukhrul, 40-year-old Sandeep Rai was shot while driving.

According to the report, Kuki-Naga tension has grown since an incident in Ukhrul in February, and more than 40 people have been killed since then. All this comes on top of the Meitei and Kuki-Zo conflict running since May 2023, in which more than 300 lives were lost and more than 59 thousand people were displaced.
nazar: Manipur's fire is now spreading along a new fault line: two Adivasi (indigenous) communities that have lived together in the hills are facing off. Even after three years the state has neither gathered the weapons nor restored trust. Armed 'volunteers' formed to protect villages are now themselves becoming a cause of conflict. Amid the Delhi headlines, it is the duty of both the media and Parliament to see that these deaths are not lost in a line or two.
sawal: Who will talk of peace in Manipur, and when?
ref: Village volunteers
Ordinary people in Manipur's villages who took up arms for self-defence after the 2023 conflict. The government considers them illegal armed groups.
Kuki and Naga
Two major Adivasi (indigenous) communities of Manipur's hill areas. There have been old tensions between them over land and territory.

h: Scholars step forward for the release of Imaan Mazari and Hadi Chattha
dek: Ten professors of Pakistani origin in the US and Britain called the 17-year sentence for social media posts an attack on free expression.
body: Scholars of Pakistani origin teaching at universities in the US and Britain have issued a joint statement for the release of Pakistani human rights lawyer Imaan Zainab Mazari-Hazir and lawyer Hadi Ali Chattha. According to Dawn, the initiative was taken by Aqil Shah of Georgetown University, and the signatories include names such as Ayesha Jalal, Ayesha Siddiqa, Raza Rumi and Yunus Samad.

According to the statement, both were sentenced to 17 years in January 2026 under the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA). Their crime was criticising alleged human rights abuses on social media. On 17 September the Supreme Court suspended the sentence and granted bail, but within a few hours police detained them again in a separate case, and they remain in custody.

The scholars recalled that Mazari spoke out against enforced disappearances, advocated for victims' families and openly challenged the establishment. Chattha has fought the cases of people accused of blasphemy and of prisoners sentenced to death.

The statement says criminal law must not become a weapon to suppress dissent or intimidate lawyers. Citing the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, they said Pakistan is bound to protect the right to criticise state institutions. Related reports in Dawn say an anti-terrorism court in Islamabad has also framed charges against both in a separate security-violation case.
nazar: This story will not seem unfamiliar on this side of the border either: arrest in a new case as soon as bail is granted, years of prison for social media posts, and lawyers who fight the cases of the weak as the first targets. Turning the legal process itself into punishment is a shared disease in South Asia. Standing with rights defenders across the border is therefore part of the politics of peace.
sawal: If the lawyers themselves are in jail, who will speak for the victims?
ref: PECA
Pakistan's Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act, 2016. Critics say it is used to criminalise online criticism by journalists and activists.
Imaan Mazari
A human rights lawyer in Islamabad, known for advocating for the families of missing Baloch and Pashtun people.

h: The sea swallowed homes, displacement swallowed bonds: the ache of Pozhiyoor
dek: Fishing families uprooted by erosion on the Thiruvananthapuram coast reached new flats, but loneliness and depression came with them.
body: Kulathoor, the southernmost panchayat of Kerala's Thiruvananthapuram district, has faced sea erosion for decades. According to this Mongabay India report, in coastal wards such as Pozhiyoor and Kollamcode, where there were once about a hundred rows of houses, only seven or eight rows remain. Even stone sea walls could not stop the waves. According to a 2022 study cited in the report, about 2.62 square kilometres of land was eroded here in 14 years, and in Pozhiyoor erosion runs at more than ten and a half metres a year. On 28 September a sea surge brought down 40 more houses.

The state's Punargeham scheme gives fishing families living within 50 metres of the shore up to ten lakh rupees for land, a house or a flat. 128 families from Kulathoor were resettled in the Niravu flats at Karode, seven kilometres away. But the report shows that the distance made access to the sea, work, worship and daily expenses all harder.

At a medical camp in Pozhiyoor in 2025, a psychiatrist found symptoms of trauma and depression in most people. A fisherman living in the flats now hardly gets to meet his friends; elderly women who earned by drying fish now have neither space nor work. Resettlement has not been even either, which has bred bitterness in the community. According to parish records, about 400 people are still waiting for a safe home, while the government has no official account of the losses.

The local church has started a counselling initiative with volunteers and a hospital. An anthropologist quoted in the report says that until the environmental damage is made good, the wounds of the mind will not fully heal either.
nazar: The debate on the climate crisis often stops at figures for cement, walls and compensation. This report reminds us that for fishing people the coast is not just land but a place of work, neighbourhood and faith. If resettlement schemes do not count these bonds, even the people who are saved will stay uprooted inside. Along India's long coastline there are hundreds of Pozhiyoors like this, and they are not even being counted.
sawal: Is resettlement only about giving a roof, or also about giving back a life?
ref: Coastal erosion
The gradual washing away of shoreline land by waves, currents and rising sea levels. Structures such as harbours and walls often speed it up in nearby areas.
Punargeham
A Kerala government scheme that gives money to resettle fishing families living very close to the sea in safer places.

h: A library in every village: a Tamil poet's demand
dek: Remembering the world books built for him, Chennai poet Arul Raj asks why libraries have not reached children in villages and Adivasi areas.
body: Published in PARI's 'Things We Do' section, this piece is half essay and half poem. Chennai writer Arul Raj recalls a time when pictures and videos were not easy to come by and books were the only window to the outside world. What he read beyond his school lessons widened his view and made him a writer.

He mentions Chennai's Anna Centenary Library and the old Connemara Public Library, and recalls that Tamil Nadu passed a public libraries law in 1948, just a year after independence. It was the first state in the country to do so. According to the Directorate of Public Libraries, set up in 1972, the state today has about 4,640 public libraries.

But the picture behind the figures is not as good. According to the writer, many people in rural, hill and Adivasi (indigenous) areas do not even know what a library is. Many government schools have no librarian post, no separate reading room and no separate budget for books.

So his demand is clear: there should be a library in every village and every town, because school education alone is not enough. He draws on the thinking of the great poet Subramania Bharati, who spoke of spreading knowledge and fostering a broad outlook.

The piece comes with his poem 'Library', in both Tamil and English, along with audio in which P. Sainath reads the English version. The poem sees the library as a place where different scriptures live together in peace, where one travels without passport or ticket. Read and listen to the poem on the original page.
nazar: When books and librarians are the first to be cut from the education budget, the children who lose most are those with not a single book at home. Tamil Nadu's 1948 law shows this can be done with government will. For Dalit, Adivasi and first-generation readers, a village library is not a hobby but the first step towards equality.
sawal: When did the last library open in your village or neighbourhood?
ref: Connemara Public Library

Chennai's historic public library, opened in 1896.
It is one of the four libraries in the country that receive a copy of every book published in India.
Subramania Bharati

A great Tamil poet and freedom fighter (1882-1921).
His poems on anti-caste struggle, women's education and freedom are still sung today.
photo_note: An illustrated manuscript of the Kalpasutra

h: South Andaman: fewer fish, more plastic
dek: Small fishers of Neil Island describe how big trawlers from Port Blair, ghost nets and plastic have squeezed their earnings.
body: When the Mandal family of Neil Island (Shaheed Dweep) returned at the end of April after two days at sea, they had only ten kilos of fish. Five years ago a single day's trip brought in at least twenty kilos. According to fisherman Tulsi Mandal, dinghies once landed 50 to 100 kilos a day; now a crew of three or four is lucky to get 20 kilos in deep water.

The fall in fish near the shore has put the livelihood of more than a hundred families at stake. People go more than 50 kilometres out into unfamiliar waters in small wooden boats, and now set out almost every day instead of twice a week. There is no cold storage on the island, so the catch often has to be thrown away.

The fishers allege that big boats from Port Blair stay at sea for five or six days, follow small boats to find their spots, and even catch protected species there. When the trawlers' heavy nets get snagged, they are cut and left behind, floating as waste on the reefs and in the water.

These ghost nets tangle with small boats; by Harish Mondal's count, repairs and bait cost about ten thousand rupees extra a year. In April 2025, divers from the Kachrewale Foundation pulled 500 square metres of net out of the sea. Plastic found in fish stomachs has also shaken customers' trust.

The report says much of the waste here drifts in from Port Blair, the mainland and neighbouring countries. The Mandal family is among the Bengali families who came from Bangladesh after Partition and were settled here in the 1950s, and today its monthly income is 13 to 15 thousand rupees.
nazar: The Andamans are usually discussed in terms of ports, tourism and 'development' projects, but the small fishers who have the first claim on the sea stay outside that debate. Curbs on big trawlers, cold storage and joint work with neighbouring countries on marine waste are not small demands; they are the conditions for their survival.
sawal: Whose sea is it, the trawler's or the dinghy's?
ref: Ghost nets

Fishing nets abandoned or lost at sea.
They drift for years, trapping fish, turtles and boats.
Neil Island

A small island in South Andaman, now called Shaheed Dweep.
A large part of its population is made up of resettled Bengali families.

h: The Bhopas of Churu: settled at last, but rights still far away
dek: A Bhopa family that once roamed playing the ravanhatha has lived in a Rajasthan village for eleven years, but the fight for electricity, pensions and identity goes on.
body: Bhadar Bhopa, 65, spent most of his life on the move, playing the ravanhatha and singing. About eleven years ago he stopped with his five sons in Dheerwas Bada village in Churu district, because he often passed through and people knew him. This report is by PARI student reporter Pramod Indaliya, who studied at the same school the family's children attended.

The family links itself to the Nayak community, which is a Scheduled Caste, while in Rajasthan Bhopas are counted as OBC and the Nayaks hesitate to accept them. For the first two years they lived outside the village; then the sarpanch (village head) gave them about three quarters of an acre. Today a clan of about 50 people lives in mud houses on part of the haddwar, the place where dead cattle are dumped.

At first the villagers did not trust them with work. Only when a Brahmin farmer called them in as his harvest ran late did others also start giving them work. Even so, unlike other communities, their wages are not fixed; every time they must bargain over hours and pay. People go 150 kilometres away to Sikar for the onion harvest, and children leave school to go along.

The settlement has no electricity; a connection 500 metres away has not reached it. Bhadar and his wife Kamla struggle to get their old-age pension because of digital KYC and bank mergers. The government dashboard declares the village open defecation free, but the family did not get money for a toilet, and the Har Ghar Jal tap dried up in a few months.

In the Special Intensive Revision of the voter list, his son Bhagirath had to give up a day's wages at his hotel job in Meerut and come back to prove residence. Now only Bhadar and Bhanwar Lal in the whole family can play the ravanhatha.
nazar: For nomadic and denotified communities, 'settling down' does not by itself bring rights. Papers, the tangle of caste categories and digital KYC: at every step they must prove again that they belong to this very country. In this season of voter list revision, the story shows who bears the heaviest burden.
sawal: How many years should it take someone who wants to settle to prove who they are?
ref: Bhopa

A nomadic community of Rajasthan and Gujarat that sings the ballads of folk deities.
Telling the story with a ravanhatha before the phad (painted scroll) of Pabuji has been their mark.
Ravanhatha

A bowed folk instrument made of bamboo and coconut shell.
It is counted among India's oldest string instruments.

h: Gen Z's Gandhi: an old tool returns to Jantar Mantar
dek: This documentary by The Hindu shows how the young people of the Cockroach movement arrived at Gandhi's methods without reading Gandhi: the sit-in, the fast, and not raising a hand even when beaten.
body: The film begins in the summer of 2026, when young people sat down at Jantar Mantar after the NEET paper leak. A remark by the Chief Justice had called unemployed youth cockroaches, and they made that insult their identity. A page that began with a tweet reached crores of people, then became an organisation, then a sit-in.

No one had decided which day would be a sit-in and which a fast. The film's intriguing claim is that this generation did not come to Gandhi through reading him, yet picked up his very tools. Tushar Gandhi says his generation, betrayed by the Anna movement, was suspicious at first, but Neha Bora's 23-day fast, in which Gandhi's name was not mentioned once, removed his doubts.

Historian Ramachandra Guha recalls that for Gandhi non-violence was not only a moral matter but a political understanding: if you use violence, a more powerful government will use more violence, and the ordinary person will be crushed in between. The film also traces the journey of this method from Mandela in South Africa to the American civil rights movement.

Gopalkrishna Gandhi offers praise along with a word of advice: abusive language crept into the movement in places, which Gandhi would have been upset by, and it weakens the movement. The film also records that Gandhi and Ambedkar were together on the posters at Jantar Mantar: the slogans Ambedkar's, the method Gandhi's.

The last part goes, through SEWA's Mirai Chatterjee, to Gandhi's less discussed work of slowly organising people: a Dalit health worker with a disability, from whose hand upper-caste men of the village had refused to take medicine, was finally elected sarpanch (head) of that same village.
nazar: The strength of this film is that it sees Gandhi not as a statue but as a method: not turning violent even while angry, and not becoming like the one you are fighting. Today, when Delhi has been turned into a fortress and young people are being taken off trains, the question of how long unarmed resolve can hold out against the baton of power has become even more urgent.

But the film also reminds us that Gandhi's talisman, remembering the face of the poorest and weakest person, is the real test of any movement. This fight for the right to vote will be complete only when it also includes the people whose names were the first to be cut from the list: Dalits, Muslims, migrant workers and women.
sawal: How does someone reach Gandhi's path without reading Gandhi?
ref: Gandhi's talisman
Gandhi's test: whenever you take a decision, recall the face of the poorest and weakest person and ask what it will give him.
SEWA
The Self Employed Women's Association, an organisation of women workers in the unorganised sector, founded by Ela Bhatt in Gujarat in 1972.

h: Anne Carson: the art of leaping into the dark
dek: A Hindi translation of an old conversation with Nobel winner Anne Carson, in which she talks about error, translation and everyday light.
body: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature has gone to Anne Carson, the Canadian poet, translator and classics scholar. On this occasion Samalochan has published in Hindi her conversation with Kate Dwyer that appeared in The Paris Review in 2024. The translation is by Anurag Ankur, who also adds a note.

The conversation begins with the title of her book 'Wrong Norma'. Carson says the academic world breeds a constant fear of being proved wrong, and she wanted to turn that fear around. Citing Simone Weil, she says contradictions loosen the grip of thought; being wrong does the same.

For her, language is a very private thing. No one fully understands another, so every relationship is a constant translation, and speaking is like jumping into the dark. In translation she is drawn to the gap between the original and the new language. That is why she finds the many versions of a single Emily Dickinson poem beautiful.

Writing, for her, begins by following an idea, like someone tracking a fox. Every day she looks for exact words about that day's light in a private notebook, and considers this the foundation of the rest of her work. Swimming, drawing and the pause of looking up a word in a printed dictionary are also part of her writing; the computer dictionary has taken that pause away.
At the end she speaks about time: being absorbed in a film, a poem or a task is like stopping time, but by her reckoning it lasts only a few minutes.
nazar: World literature often arrives in Hindi with the news of a prize and stops there. Samalochan has gone beyond the news and brought a writer's way of thinking to readers. The idea of freedom from the fear of being wrong is just as necessary for our classrooms and universities.
sawal: Can a new idea be born without the freedom to be wrong?
ref: Anne Carson

Canadian poet, essayist and translator of Greek classics, born 1950.
'Autobiography of Red' and 'Nox' are among her well-known books.
Simone Weil

French philosopher and activist (1909-1943).
She worked among labourers; her writing on attention, suffering and justice has had a deep influence.

h: The first instalment of Mrinal Pande's autobiography
dek: Mrinal Pande's autobiographical series, begun on Janaki Pul, is about memory, women's life stories and being born in the palace of Orchha.
body: Senior writer and editor Mrinal Pande has begun a series of her autobiography on Janaki Pul, with the next instalment due next week. In the first instalment she says that when she sat down to write her story at the urging of friends, readers and publishers, she felt hesitation along with enthusiasm.

Through the Sanskrit word 'vidagdha', she speaks of a person who has been ripened by the heat of life, and recalls Draupadi's sharp words in Bharavi's 'Kiratarjuniyam'. There is also mention of Banarasidas's 'Ardhakathanak', written in 1641, which is considered the first autobiography in Hindi.

Her direct question is: will today's readers and publishers read a woman's life story with the same seriousness and patience as a man's? For the writer, memory is the only measure of experience, as rhythm is for a musician. She also speaks of a stern 'yaksha' (guardian spirit) within her, who tests every draft like a potter.

No ancestral home, no inheritance, no family library; what is truly her own is this inner witness. She was born in the palace of Orchha, at her mother's parents' home, and as a second daughter her arrival was not considered welcome. After a BA from Shantiniketan she was married young to a widower who had a daughter.

Relatives kept scratching at old wounds on happy occasions under the pretext of sympathy, especially about not having a son, even though she was a successful writer. The instalment ends with the Upanishadic image of the bird with two heads: one lives, the other watches and records.
nazar: Women's autobiographies in Hindi are still few, and those that exist are often set aside as 'personal'. Mrinal Pande places the craving for a son and the unwantedness of a second daughter as a public question. This series could become a mirror for Hindi society.
sawal: Why do we call a woman's autobiography 'personal'?
ref: Ardhakathanak

An autobiography written in Braj Bhasha in 1641 by the Jain merchant-poet Banarasidas.
It is considered the first autobiography in Hindi.
Mrinal Pande

A writer and journalist in Hindi and English, former editor of Hindustan.
She has also been chair of Prasar Bharati; she is the daughter of the writer Shivani.

h: Gurudev and the Mahatma: respect alongside disagreement
dek: In Hindwi's 'C/O Bengal' series, Baby Shaw sees the relationship between Tagore and Gandhi as an example of open debate and deep respect.
body: This part of the 'C/O Bengal' series running in Hindwi's Bela section opens with a scene from 29 May 1925: Rabindranath's elder brother Dwijendranath Tagore is praising Gandhi's patience in the face of hard questions, and Gandhi has left his chair to sit at his feet.

Gandhi was then touring Bengal with the message of the charkha (spinning wheel), as a symbol of swadeshi, the dignity of labour and self-reliance. Tagore doubted that a mechanical practice could become the symbol of a whole nation's freedom. According to the writer, Tagore's respect was genuine, but it did not mean agreement, and the conversation went on regardless.

The piece recalls Gandhi and Kasturba's first visit to Shantiniketan in 1915, when Tagore was not there. Gandhi suggested that teachers and students do their daily chores themselves. The experiment did not last long, but 10 March is still marked there as 'Gandhi Day'. Tagore is credited with calling Gandhi 'Mahatma', and Gandhi called him 'Gurudev'.

The disagreements are recorded too: the 1921 boycott, the bonfires of foreign cloth and the centrality of the charkha did not sit well with Tagore. Yet in 1932, during Gandhi's fast in Yerwada jail over separate electorates for Dalits, Tagore sent a telegram and went to Pune. In 1936 Gandhi helped raise funds for Visva-Bharati, and in 1940 Tagore asked him to look after Visva-Bharati.
The writer concludes that this relationship shows principled disagreement is possible without enmity, while in today's politics differences instantly turn into personal attacks.
nazar: Today dissent has come to be seen as sedition and criticism as enmity. In such a time, the debate between Gandhi and Tagore reminds us that the freedom struggle itself was built on open debate. That tradition is the real capital of the Constitution and of democracy.
sawal: Can we respect someone even while disagreeing with them?
ref: Poona Pact (1932)

An agreement between Ambedkar and Gandhi after Gandhi's Yerwada fast against separate electorates for Dalits.
It set reserved seats in place of separate electorates.
Visva-Bharati

The university Tagore built at Shantiniketan, founded in 1921.
It became a central university in 1951, after independence.
photo_note: Rabindranath in the role of a blind singer

h: DTC strike: a commuter's diary from the road
dek: On the day of Delhi's bus strike, a writer who travels by bus every day looks at the drivers' rights and the commuters' troubles side by side.
body: Published in Hindwi's Bela section, this memoir-essay by Sunaina begins with a simple point: we value sunlight, air and water only when they are taken away. The laws of nature are not in our hands, but public services are run by people, so why are they not run with fairness?

The writer travels by DTC bus every day. For many people in Delhi the bus is not a convenience but a necessity. On the day of the strike she had no prior notice. The bus was stopped at the Nehru Place depot, and arguing with the driver got nowhere.

She considers the strike a legitimate right and lists the drivers' demands: higher daily wages, equal pay for equal work, leave pay, bonus, medical care and social security, and an end to fines for damage to buses. In her view these demands are fair and settling them is the transport department's job.

That day the metro was packed, and the shared auto fare went from twenty rupees to a hundred. The writer could neither pay such a fare nor wait for hours, so she walked home. Amid the crowd, seeing a father delighted to ride the metro with his daughter for the first time was a different sight that day.

At the end come questions: why did it come to a strike, why were commuters not told, will it happen again? She also records that drivers earn about 862 rupees a day, while many commuters earn even less, so whose strike would it take for them to be heard?
nazar: The fight of worker against commuter is really the government's failure, which gives neither the drivers proper pay nor the city enough buses. The strength of this essay is that it does not make either side a villain in anger. Contract drivers and low-earning commuters belong to the same class of people.
sawal: When public transport stops, who is the first to walk?
ref: DTC

The Delhi Transport Corporation, the capital's government bus service.
Many of its drivers and conductors work on contract.
Equal pay for equal work

The principle that people doing the same work should get the same pay.
The Supreme Court has held that it applies to contract and temporary workers too.

h: 'Kaviraj': from the peak of fame to Khoda Colony
dek: Sanjay Kundan's new story is about a famous poet-professor who, unsettled by the popularity of an unknown young poet, sets out to find him.
body: Sanjay Kundan's story 'Kaviraj' (king of poets), published on Samalochan, casts a sharp, satirical eye on the world of Hindi literature. The story is given here in summary; read the full story on the original page.

Kaviraj is a professor at Delhi University and a famous Hindi poet. His early poems won praise from a major critic, and then came awards, books, posts, a circle of disciples, and seats on award committees and editorial boards. No one speaks against him.

Then a short comment appears on the internet under the name 'Ajanand' saying that Kaviraj is repeating himself. It shakes him to the core. Ajanand's poems get published, students recite them, they are sung in a procession, an MP reads one in Parliament. Flattering disciples offer comfort, but Kaviraj's pen stops.

It turns out that Ajanand is a boy of twenty-seven or twenty-eight who lives in Khoda Colony in Ghaziabad and works in Noida. Kaviraj remembers the hardship of his youth, when poetry was born of struggle, and turns his car towards Khoda to gain a 'new experience'.

The journey from gleaming towers to mud, drains and mosquitoes is the most powerful part of the story. In the end a call comes about a housewarming party, and Kaviraj leaves the road and turns back towards comfort. Read the story itself to see how the ending unfolds.
nazar: This story questions literary power in Hindi: who holds the awards and posts, and where new, living poetry is coming from. Voices rising from settlements like Khoda are often brushed aside as 'raw'. The story shows that making struggle a subject is easy; going near it and staying is hard.
sawal: Does fame take poetry away from its own source?
ref: Khoda Colony

A dense, low-income settlement in Ghaziabad district, next to Noida.
Many working people of Delhi-NCR live here.
Sanjay Kundan

A Hindi poet, fiction writer and journalist.
He has written poetry, short stories and novels.
photo_note: The Brahmin of the Kali Yuga

h: Nana Patekar: from the anger of 'Ankush' to the laughter of Uday Shetty
dek: In Sammukh's column 'Ilmi-Filmi', Aniruddh Sharma looks back on Nana Patekar's journey from 'Ankush' to 'Welcome'.
body: In his Sammukh column 'Ilmi-Filmi', Aniruddh Sharma has written a tribute on the death of actor Nana Patekar. According to the writer, the news came suddenly; there had been no word of any illness, and admirers were waiting for some new, powerful role.

The piece recalls that Nana was among the very few actors, along with Irrfan, to win awards for a lead role, a supporting role and a villain. He began with 'Gaman' (1978), then did Marathi films, and returned to Hindi in 1984 with 'Aaj Ki Awaz', after Smita Patil persuaded him.

'Ankush' (1984) made him a name with audiences. The writer says Nana, who worked for a very small fee, also helped get the film finished. 'Salaam Bombay' (1988) brought his first National Award, and 'Thoda Sa Roomani Ho Jaayen' showed him in a direction quite opposite to his image.

His famous temper is in the piece too, with some hearsay stories that the writer himself calls unconfirmed. In 1991 he directed 'Prahaar', and the film did well, but he never directed again. The writer also recalls that in a recent interview Nana and Anil Kapoor had talked of working together again, a plan now left unfinished.

Anna Seth in 'Parinda', Shivaji Rao Wagle in 'Tirangaa', Pratap Narayan in 'Krantiveer', Majid Khan in 'Angaar' and Uday Shetty in 'Welcome': according to the writer, it is this range that keeps an actor loved for decades.
nazar: Nana Patekar's cinema, especially 'Ankush' and 'Krantiveer', gave a voice to the anger of the jobless young man and the common person. Cinema that ties that anger to a demand for justice is rarer today. Tributes like this also keep alive a tradition of Hindi film writing that looks past the star to the character.
sawal: Where does today's cinema take the common man's anger?
ref: Salaam Bombay

Mira Nair's 1988 film about street children in Mumbai.
It was nominated for an Oscar.
Prahaar

A 1991 film, the only one Nana Patekar directed.
He played an army officer, and Madhuri Dixit acted without make-up.
